title: Clouds and rain: how tiny drops in a cloud become rain

summary.text: A cloud is made of millions of tiny drops of water, each one thinner than a hair. They are so small and light that they float in the air. Rain falls only when many tiny drops join into one bigger, heavier drop. Your child tests this with a spray bottle and a steel plate: the fine mist clings to the plate, and only after many sprays does a drop grow big enough to run down. Then they find out where a cloud's water comes from, and why grey clouds are the ones that bring rain.
summary.art: A big grey monsoon cloud over a row of flats, with a zoom-in circle showing tiny round drops bumping and joining into one big raindrop that falls.

intro.hook: Spray one puff of mist from a spray bottle into the air, in a beam of torchlight. Then let one drop of water fall from a spoon. Which one reaches the floor first?
intro.text: The drop from the spoon falls straight down in a blink. The tiny drops of the mist sparkle in the light and drift slowly, and some seem to hang in the air. A cloud is made of drops even smaller than these. So how does a cloud ever make rain? In this unit you test it yourself, with a spray bottle and a steel plate.
intro.art: A dark room with a torch beam shining across it, a sparkling puff of mist drifting in the beam, and a single big drop falling from a steel spoon beside it.

outcomes: By the end I can say that a cloud is made of millions of tiny drops of water floating in the air.
By the end I can say that tiny drops fall very slowly and float, and big drops fall fast.
By the end I can explain that rain falls when many tiny drops join into bigger, heavier drops.
By the end I can say where the water in a cloud comes from: water evaporates from seas, rivers and wet things, and cools high up into tiny drops.
By the end I can say that thick grey clouds are more likely to bring rain than thin white ones, and why.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, test it, and say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: A cloud is a huge crowd of tiny drops of water, or tiny bits of ice, floating high in the air.
terms.example: The white puffy shapes in the sky on a sunny afternoon, and the dark sky before a monsoon storm, are both clouds.
terms.art: A white puffy cloud with a zoom-in circle showing thousands of tiny round drops spread far apart.

terms.meaning: One of the tiny drops a cloud is made of. It is far thinner than a hair, too small to see on its own.
terms.example: A cloud drop is about as wide as a hair split into five.
terms.art: A single hair drawn across the picture, with a row of five tiny round drops fitting across its width.

terms.meaning: A drop of water big and heavy enough to fall from a cloud to the ground.
terms.example: One raindrop holds about as much water as a million cloud drops.
terms.art: One big raindrop next to a crowd of very many tiny cloud drops, with an equals sign between them.

terms.meaning: Water as a gas. It is mixed into the air, and you cannot see it.
terms.example: The air in your kitchen holds water vapour, even when it looks clear and empty.
terms.art: A clear kitchen with faint dotted swirls in the air, labelled 'water vapour: invisible'.

terms.meaning: When water evaporates, it slowly turns from a liquid into water vapour and goes into the air.
terms.example: Wet clothes on a line dry because their water evaporates.
terms.art: Wet clothes on a balcony line in the sun, with faint wavy lines rising from them into the air.

terms.meaning: When water vapour condenses, it cools and turns back into tiny drops of liquid water.
terms.example: High in the sky, the air is cold. There, water vapour condenses into the tiny drops that make a cloud.
terms.art: Faint invisible swirls rising from the sea, turning into tiny drops and a cloud high above.

terms.meaning: The season of strong winds from the sea that bring most of India's rain.
terms.example: In Kerala, the monsoon rain usually begins in early June. In Chennai, most rain comes from October to December.
terms.art: A map of India with big arrows of wind blowing in from the sea and grey clouds over the land.

explanations.concept: A cloud is a crowd of tiny drops
explanations.context: This card says what a cloud is made of.
explanations.definition: A cloud is made of millions and millions of tiny drops of water, or tiny bits of ice, floating in the air.
explanations.description: From far away, a cloud looks soft and solid, like cotton. Up close, it is wet mist. People who walk on hills in Munnar or Shillong sometimes walk right through a cloud, and tiny drops collect on their hair. Each cloud drop is far thinner than a hair.
examples: Walking through a cloud on a hill road feels like cool, wet mist.
Tiny drops collect on your hair and clothes inside a cloud.
The mist from a spray bottle is a little like a cloud, but its drops are bigger.
explanations.art: A girl walking on a misty hill road in Munnar, with tiny shining drops on her hair and a tea garden fading into the cloud behind her.

explanations.concept: Tiny drops float, big drops fall
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the torch beam, when the mist drifted and the spoon drop fell fast.
explanations.definition: Every drop falls, but a tiny drop falls very slowly. The air pushes against it as it falls, and for a tiny drop that push matters a lot.
explanations.description: In the torch beam, the drop from the spoon fell in a blink. The tiny drops of mist drifted, and some floated for many seconds. A cloud drop is even smaller than a mist drop. It falls only about a centimetre each second, and rising air in the sky easily carries it up. A big raindrop falls several metres each second, about as fast as a person cycling. A small puffy cloud holds about 500 tonnes of water, as heavy as 100 elephants, says Peggy LeMone, a cloud scientist in the United States. Yet it floats, because that water is split into tiny, slow drops.
examples: The spoon drop fell straight to the floor.
The mist drifted slowly in the torch beam.
Dust floats in a sunbeam for the same reason: each speck is tiny and light.
explanations.art: Two drops side by side: a big drop with a long arrow pointing down, and a tiny drop with a very short arrow and a curly arrow of rising air lifting it.

explanations.concept: Rain falls when tiny drops join
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the spray plate test, when the tiny drops clung on until they joined.
explanations.definition: Inside a cloud, tiny drops bump into each other and join. When a drop has grown big and heavy enough, it falls as rain.
explanations.description: On your steel plate, the first sprays left tiny drops that stayed still. As you sprayed more, the drops grew, touched and joined. Only a big drop ran down. Inside a cloud, the same joining happens again and again. In very tall clouds the top is freezing cold, and tiny bits of ice grow there, join and fall. They melt into raindrops on the way down.
examples: On the plate, many tiny drops joined into one drop that ran down.
On a window in the rain, a big drop races down and swallows the small drops in its way.
Tall monsoon clouds have ice at the top, even on a hot day.
explanations.art: Inside a cloud: tiny drops bumping and joining into bigger and bigger drops, and the biggest one falling out of the bottom of the cloud as rain.

explanations.concept: Where a cloud's water comes from
explanations.context: This card explains how water from the sea, rivers and wet clothes ends up in a cloud.
explanations.definition: The Sun warms water in seas, rivers, ponds and wet things, and the water evaporates into the air as invisible water vapour. High in the sky the air is cold, and the vapour condenses into tiny drops. That is a cloud.
explanations.description: Water is always evaporating, from the Bay of Bengal, from the Kaveri, from a puddle and from the wet clothes on your balcony. The water vapour mixes into the air, and you cannot see it. Warm air rises, and the higher it goes, the colder it gets. When the air is cold enough, the vapour condenses into tiny drops, each one round a speck of dust or sea salt too small to see. Millions of these drops together make a cloud.
examples: Wet clothes dry because their water evaporates into the air.
Monsoon winds carry damp air from the sea over Kerala and the Western Ghats.
Rain that falls in Chennai may have evaporated from the Bay of Bengal a few days before.
explanations.art: A simple loop: the sun warming the sea, wavy invisible lines rising, a cloud forming high up over hills, and rain falling into a river that flows back to the sea.

explanations.context: This card explains why some clouds are white and others are dark grey.
explanations.definition: A thin cloud lets plenty of sunlight through, so it looks white. A very thick cloud stops most of the light before it reaches the bottom, so its underside looks grey or nearly black.
explanations.description: All clouds are made of the same clear water drops. A thick cloud has many more drops, piled up high, and so many drops spread the light out that little comes out of the bottom. A thick cloud also has more water, and its drops have more chances to join. That is why dark grey clouds are the ones that usually bring rain. Joanne Simpson, the first woman to earn a doctorate in weather science, spent her life studying tall rain clouds over warm seas.
examples: Thin white clouds on a sunny morning rarely rain.
Before a monsoon storm, the sky turns dark grey.
The top of a tall storm cloud, lit by the Sun, can look bright white while its bottom is dark.
explanations.art: Two clouds: a thin white one with lots of sunlight passing through, and a tall thick one with a bright white top and a dark grey bottom, raining.

agreed.text: Clouds are made of tiny drops of liquid water, or tiny bits of ice, floating in the air.
agreed.evidence: People in planes and on mountains have caught cloud drops and looked at them under a microscope. Walking through a cloud on a hill leaves tiny drops on your hair.

agreed.text: Rain falls when tiny cloud drops grow and join into drops heavy enough to fall.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have flown special planes through clouds to measure the drops. Clouds that are raining hold bigger drops among the tiny ones. Clouds that are not raining hold almost only tiny drops.

agreed.text: The water in clouds comes from water that evaporated from seas, rivers, lakes, soil, plants and wet things.
agreed.evidence: The water that evaporates and the water that falls as rain balance out over the whole Earth, year after year.

challenging.claim: Clouds are made of smoke, or of something like cotton.
challenging.who: A common guess by young children
challenging.for: From far away, clouds look soft and fluffy, and some look like smoke from a chimney.
challenging.against: Walk through a cloud on a hill, and you come out with damp hair. Cloud drops have been caught and looked at under microscopes: they are water.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess on what clouds are made of.

challenging.claim: The specks in a cloud are tiny hollow bubbles, filled with air, like soap bubbles.
challenging.who: Many scientists in Europe in the 1700s, such as Horace-Bénédict de Saussure
challenging.for: A hollow bubble would be very light, so it would explain why a cloud floats.
challenging.against: In 1846, Augustus Waller looked at mist through a microscope and saw solid round drops, not bubbles. Today we know cloud drops float because they are tiny, and rising air holds them up.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that turned out wrong.

challenging.claim: Raindrops are shaped like tears, with a pointed top.
challenging.for: A drop hanging from a tap, just before it falls, has a pointed top.
challenging.against: Photos taken with very fast cameras show falling raindrops are round when small. Big ones get squashed flat at the bottom by the air, a little like a burger bun.
challenging.context: This card is about the shape of a falling raindrop.

challenging.claim: People can make clouds rain by 'seeding' them: spraying tiny specks of salt or other powders into them from planes.
challenging.who: Scientists who test cloud seeding, in India and other countries
challenging.for: Tests show the right clouds sometimes give more rain after seeding. Scientists from the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology in Pune have tested it over Solapur in Maharashtra.
challenging.against: Seeding only works on clouds that already hold plenty of water. It cannot make rain from a clear sky. It is also hard to know how much rain would have fallen anyway.
challenging.context: This card is about whether people can make it rain.

big_questions.q: Why do some clouds rain, and others float away without a drop?
big_questions.hint: On the plate, what had to happen before a drop ran down?

big_questions.q: The water in your glass may once have been in a cloud over the sea. Where else might it have been?
big_questions.hint: Think of rivers, plants, animals, and people breathing out.

big_questions.q: When a cloud rains itself away, has the cloud gone, or has it just changed?
big_questions.hint: Where did all its water go?

big_questions.q: Is a cloud one thing, or millions of things?
big_questions.hint: Each drop floats on its own. Yet we give them all one name.

how_we_found_out.story: If clouds are made of water, why do they float? Water is much heavier than air. In the 1700s, many scientists in Europe had an answer. They said the specks in a cloud are tiny hollow bubbles, like soap bubbles, filled with air. A hollow bubble is very light, so it floats. Horace-Bénédict de Saussure, a Swiss scientist who climbed the Alps to study the air, believed in the bubbles too. Then, in 1846, Augustus Waller, a doctor in London, looked at the mist above hot water through a microscope. He saw solid round drops, not hollow bubbles. He sent his findings to the Royal Society, a famous science society in London, and they were printed in 1847. Other scientists agreed with him in the years after. Today we know a cloud is made of solid water drops. They float because they are so tiny that they fall very slowly, and rising air carries them up.
how_we_found_out.who: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure, a Swiss scientist who believed cloud specks were bubbles, and Augustus Waller, a doctor in London who looked at them with a microscope
how_we_found_out.when: The 1700s (the bubble idea) and 1846 (Waller's microscope study, printed in 1847)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That cloud specks are tiny hollow bubbles filled with air, which is why they float. Waller's microscope showed solid round drops instead.
how_we_found_out.art: A young man in 1840s clothes looking down a brass microscope at a glass slide, with a steaming bowl of hot water beside him, and a circle showing what he sees: solid round drops.

story.title: The Bag in the Sky
story.note: Meenakshi, Karthik, Amma and Paati are made up. Amma works as a weather scientist. The northeast monsoon really does bring Chennai most of its rain between October and December.
text: It was November in Chennai, and the sky over the flats had been grey all morning. Meenakshi was seven. Her little brother Karthik was five. They sat at the window and watched the clouds.
"When is the rain coming?" asked Karthik. "The clouds are full. Why don't they burst?"
"Burst?" said Meenakshi.
"Like a bag of water," said Karthik. "A cloud is a big bag, full of rain. When it gets too full, it bursts. Paati said the sky will open today."
Paati laughed from the kitchen. "That is only a way of saying it, kanna. Ask your Amma. Clouds are her work."

Amma worked at the weather office in Chennai. She studied clouds and rain all day, and she was home early because of the storm warning. She came over with a spray bottle, the one Paati used for ironing clothes, and a steel plate.
"Let us find out what is inside a cloud," Amma said. "Meenakshi, you can be the scientist. Karthik, you can be the counter."
Meenakshi stood the plate on its edge on a tray, leaning against the wall. Amma turned the nozzle of the bottle until it made the finest mist.

"A cloud is made of tiny drops of water," said Amma. "Millions of them. Each one is thinner than a hair. This mist is a little like a cloud. Its drops are tiny too, though a cloud's are tinier still. Now, Meenakshi, if you spray the plate, what will the water do?"
"It will run down," said Meenakshi. "Water always runs down."
"Let us see. One spray at a time."
Meenakshi sprayed once. The shiny plate went dull, as if someone had breathed on it. She bent close. The plate was covered in tiny drops, like grains of rava. Not one of them moved.
"They are stuck," said Karthik.
"Spray again," said Amma. "Karthik, count."
Two. Three. Four. Five. The tiny drops grew fatter. Here and there, two drops touched and became one. Six. Seven. Eight. Now the drops were as big as mustard seeds. Nine. Ten.

At the eleventh spray, one drop near the top touched its neighbour, then another. Suddenly it was too big to hold on. It slid down the plate, fast, and on the way it swallowed every little drop in its path. It left a clean, shining line behind it.
"It fell!" shouted Karthik. "Eleven!"
"Why did that drop fall, and the others did not?" asked Amma.
Meenakshi thought. "The small ones were too small. They just stayed. When lots of them joined together, the drop got big and heavy. Then it fell."

"That is what a scientist would say," said Amma. "Let us try again, to check it was not luck." Meenakshi wiped the plate dry and sprayed again. This time the first drop ran down at fourteen sprays. The third time, at twelve.
"So the cloud is not a bag?" asked Karthik.

"No bag," said Meenakshi. Now she was the one explaining. "A cloud is all tiny drops, floating. They are too small to fall. Inside the cloud they bump and join, like on the plate. When a drop is big enough, it falls. That is a raindrop."
Karthik frowned. "But how many little drops make one raindrop?"
"About a million," said Amma. "Far more than you could ever count."
Just then there was a soft tapping on the window. Then the tapping became a roar. The rain had come.

The two children pressed their noses to the glass. On the outside of the window, small raindrops sat still, as the mist had on the plate. Then a big drop came racing down from the top. It ran into a small drop and swallowed it, and ran faster. It swallowed another, and another.
"Look, Karthik," said Meenakshi. "The window is doing our plate test."
Karthik watched for a long time. Then he said, "The cloud did not burst. It just let go of its big drops, one by one."
Paati brought them hot sundal in steel bowls. "So the sky did not open after all?" she asked, smiling.
"No, Paati," said Karthik, with his mouth full. "The drops joined."
story.epiphany: A cloud is not a bag of rain. It is millions of tiny drops, too small to fall. Rain falls when many tiny drops join into one drop heavy enough to fall.
ask: What did Karthik think a cloud was, at the start?
On the plate, why did the tiny drops stay still at first?
Why did Amma ask Meenakshi to do the test three times?
What did the big drop on the window do to the small drops in its way?
art: A Chennai flat on a grey November afternoon: a girl spraying mist on a steel plate leaning against a wall, a small boy counting on his fingers, and their mother kneeling beside them with a smile.
Two children with their noses pressed to a rainy window, watching one big drop race down and swallow the smaller drops in its path.

experiments.title: The Spray Plate: how many sprays until a drop runs down?
experiments.context: In this experiment you spray a fine mist onto a steel plate, one spray at a time. You count how many sprays it takes before a drop grows big enough to run down. It shows how a cloud's tiny drops turn into rain.
experiments.question: When tiny drops of mist land on a plate, do they run down straight away? How many sprays does it take before a drop runs down?
experiments.predict: When I spray the plate once, will the water run down straight away? How many sprays do you think it will take before a drop runs down? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We stand the plate the same way each time, and spray from the same distance, one ruler length away. We spray once at a time and count every spray. We wipe the plate dry before each try. We do three tries, because one try can be just by chance.
results_table: Sprays until the first drop ran down
What the drops looked like before that

materials.item: a spray bottle that makes a fine mist, such as the one used for ironing clothes or for plants, filled with water
materials.buy: If you have none, a small plastic spray bottle is cheap at a hardware or plastics shop. Or dip an old toothbrush in water and run your thumb over the bristles to flick a fine spray.

materials.item: a steel plate, or the flat lid of a steel dabba
a tray or an old newspaper to stand the plate on
a ruler or a 30 cm scale
a dry cloth or towel
paper and a pencil for tally marks

schedule.what: Guess. Spray the plate one spray at a time and count until a drop runs down. Do it three times. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Write your guess. Make one tally mark for each spray. Circle the spray when the first drop ran down. Draw the plate after 2 sprays, and just before the drop ran.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Sprays until a drop ran down
rows: Tiny dots like rava, then fat drops like mustard seeds
The same: tiny dots first, then they joined
The big drop swallowed the small drops on its way down

setup.art: A steel plate standing on its edge on a tray, leaning against a wall, with a spray bottle held one ruler length away from it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the plate against a wall. Hold the bottle one ruler away.

setup.art: Close-up of the steel plate covered in tiny dull dots of water after one spray, none of them moving.
setup.caption: 2. Spray once. Look closely. Do the drops move?

setup.art: A child spraying the plate again and again while a grown-up makes tally marks on paper.
setup.caption: 3. Spray one at a time. Make a tally mark for each spray.

setup.art: Close-up of the plate with bigger drops, and one drop running down and leaving a clean shining line.
setup.caption: 4. Stop when the first drop runs down. Count the marks.

flow.do: 1. Do this in the kitchen or bathroom, where a wet wall does not matter. 2. Stand the plate on its edge on the tray, leaning against the wall. 3. Turn the nozzle to its finest mist. 4. Show your child the plate and the bottle.
flow.say: I am going to spray a fine mist onto this plate, one spray at a time. Will the water run down straight away? How many sprays will it take? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the plate and the spray bottle. Will the water run down at once? Guess how many sprays. Say why.

ask.q: How many sprays will it take? Why?
good: One, because water always runs down.
Lots, because the mist is tiny.
A few, because the drops have to get bigger.

flow.parent: Don't say if the guess is right. Many children say one spray, because water always runs down. Write the guess down.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the bottle one ruler length from the plate. 2. They spray once. 3. You both look closely at the plate from the side.
flow.say: Spray once. Now look very closely. What is on the plate? Is anything moving?
flow.kid: Spray once. Look very closely at the plate. What do you see? Does anything move?

ask.q: What do you see on the plate?
good: Tiny dots of water.
The plate looks dull, like when you breathe on it.
Nothing is running down.

flow.parent: After one spray, the plate goes dull and is covered in tiny drops. None of them move. If the bottle shoots a jet, not a mist, turn the nozzle or stand further back.

flow.do: 1. Your child sprays one spray at a time, with a short wait between. 2. You make one tally mark for each spray. 3. Stop when the first drop runs down. 4. Count the marks together.
flow.say: Keep spraying, one at a time. I will make a mark for each spray. Watch the drops. Shout stop when one runs down.
flow.kid: Spray again, one at a time. Watch the drops grow. Shout stop when one runs down.

ask.q: What happened to the tiny drops as you kept spraying?
good: They got bigger.
Two drops touched and became one.
The big drop ran down and took the small ones with it.

flow.parent: Most bottles take somewhere between 5 and 30 sprays, depending on the bottle and the plate. Any number is a real result. Look for drops touching and joining.

flow.do: 1. Wipe the plate completely dry. 2. Do the test again, from the same distance, counting every spray. 3. Dry it and do it a third time. 4. Write all three numbers in the table.
flow.say: Let us do it twice more, the same way, in case the first try was just by chance. Did you get the same number each time?
flow.kid: Wipe the plate dry. Do it again. Then once more. Write your three numbers.

ask.q: Were the three numbers the same?
good: Close, but not exactly the same.
It always took many sprays, never just one.

flow.parent: The numbers will be close but not the same. That is normal. What matters is that it always takes many sprays before a drop runs down.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child why the tiny drops stayed still and what made one run down. 2. Then tell them about clouds. 3. Take one big drop on the tip of a spoon, about as big as a pea. Touch it to the dry plate near the top and watch it run.
flow.say: Why did the first sprays not run down? What had to happen first? Now watch one big drop from a spoon. A cloud is made of drops even tinier than the mist.
flow.kid: Why did the tiny drops stay still? What made one run down? Now watch a big spoon drop.

ask.q: What has to happen in a cloud before rain falls?
good: The tiny drops have to join into a big drop.
The drop has to get heavy enough to fall.

flow.parent: Wait for your child's reason before you explain. A big drop like this usually runs down at once, because it is already big and heavy. If it clings, add a second drop to it. Tiny drops cling on until many have joined.

check.q: Why did the tiny drops from the first spray stay on the plate?
options: They were too small and light to run down
check.why: Each tiny drop was too small and light to run down. Only when many joined into one big drop did it slide. Mist is water: you saw the drops join into a running drop.

experiments.title: Raindrops in Atta: are all raindrops the same size?
experiments.context: In this experiment you catch real raindrops in a plate of flour. Each drop makes a little ball of dough, so you can see how big it was. Do it on a rainy day, from a balcony or a window. You need a rainy day. If it is not raining, keep this for the next rainy day.
experiments.question: Are all raindrops the same size, or are some big and some small?
experiments.predict: When we catch raindrops in flour, will all the dough balls be the same size? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We hold the plate out for just 3 seconds, so the drops don't land on top of each other. We use a smooth, flat layer of flour. We sort the balls by size only after they have dried a little.

materials.item: a steel plate with a rim
atta or maida, enough to cover the plate about one finger deep
a tea strainer or a small sieve
a sheet of paper with three circles drawn on it: small, medium, big
a rainy day, and a balcony or a window with grills

experiments.safety: A grown-up holds the plate out, and the child stays inside the balcony railing or behind the window grill. Don't do this in a thunderstorm with lightning.

schedule.what: On a rainy day, hold the flour plate out in the rain for 3 seconds. Leave it indoors for 20 minutes while the balls firm up. Then sieve them out and sort them by size.

experiments.record: Draw the three circles. Put the dough balls in the right circle and count them. Write the numbers under each circle.

setup.art: A steel plate filled with a smooth flat layer of white flour, on a balcony ledge, with rain falling outside.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the plate with flour, one finger deep. Smooth it flat.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand holding the flour plate out past a balcony railing into the rain, with a child counting 'one, two, three' beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Hold it out in the rain for 3 seconds.

setup.art: Small dough balls of different sizes being sieved out of flour with a tea strainer and sorted onto three circles drawn on paper.
setup.caption: 3. Wait 20 minutes. Sieve out the balls and sort them.

flow.do: 1. Fill the plate with flour, about one finger deep. 2. Smooth it flat with the back of a spoon. 3. Draw three circles on paper: small, medium, big.
flow.say: Each raindrop that lands in the flour will make a little ball of dough. Will all the balls be the same size? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each raindrop will make a dough ball. Will they all be the same size? Say why.

ask.q: Will all the raindrops be the same size?
good: Yes, because they all come from the same cloud.
No, because some drops joined more than others.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Write it down.

flow.do: 1. Hold the plate out in the rain, flat. 2. Your child counts to three slowly. 3. Bring it in at once.
flow.say: Count to three with me, slowly. One, two, three. In it comes!
flow.kid: Count to three slowly while the grown-up holds the plate out.
flow.parent: In heavy rain, 1 or 2 seconds is enough. In light drizzle, 5 seconds. You want separate dots, not a soggy mess.

flow.do: 1. Take the plate in at once. 2. Put it somewhere dry indoors and do not shake it. 3. Leave it for 20 minutes, so the dough balls firm up.
flow.say: Now we wait 20 minutes, so the dough balls can firm up. While we wait, watch the rain from the window.
flow.kid: Wait 20 minutes. Watch the rain from the window.
flow.wait: Leave the plate for at least 20 minutes before sieving.

flow.do: 1. Gently sieve the flour with a tea strainer. 2. Your child sorts the balls onto the three circles. 3. Count the balls in each circle together.
flow.say: Let us sieve out the balls. Put each one in the right circle. Which circle has the most?
flow.kid: Sieve out the dough balls. Put each one in a circle. Count them.

ask.q: Which size did you find most of?
good: Small ones.
There were many sizes, not just one.

flow.do: Ask your child why the raindrops were different sizes.
flow.say: Why were some raindrops big and some small? Think about the spray plate.
flow.kid: Why were some drops big and some small? Think about the plate.

ask.q: Why are raindrops different sizes?
good: Some drops joined with more drops than others.
A big drop swallowed lots of little ones on the way down.

flow.parent: Raindrops grow by joining, and each drop meets a different number of others, so sizes vary.

check.q: Why were the raindrops in the flour different sizes?
options: Each drop had joined a different number of tiny drops
Big drops come from big clouds only
check.why: Raindrops grow by joining. Some join many tiny drops, some join fewer, so they end up different sizes. The flour only shows how big each one was.

activities.title: Mist in the Torch Beam: do tiny drops fall as fast as big ones?
activities.context: In this activity you spray a puff of mist into a torch beam in a dark room, and drop one big drop from a spoon. You watch which falls faster.

materials.item: a spray bottle that makes a fine mist
a torch, or the torch on a phone
a steel spoon and a cup of water
a room you can make dark, with a floor that can get a little wet

setup.art: A dark room with a torch lying on a table, its beam shining sideways across the room at head height.
setup.caption: 1. Make the room dark. Shine the torch sideways.

setup.art: A puff of sparkling mist drifting slowly in the torch beam, and a single big drop falling fast from a spoon beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Spray mist into the beam. Then drop water from a spoon.

flow.do: 1. Close the curtains and switch off the lights. 2. Put the torch on a table so its beam shines sideways across the room.
flow.say: I am going to spray a puff of mist into the light. Then I will drop one big drop from a spoon. Which will reach the floor first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the torch beam. Mist or a spoon drop: which falls first? Say why.

ask.q: Which will reach the floor first?
good: The spoon drop, because it is big.
The same, because both are water.

flow.do: 1. Spray one puff of mist into the beam, at head height. 2. Count slowly how long you can see it in the light. 3. Then tip one drop off a spoon at the same height, through the beam.
flow.say: Watch the mist sparkle. Count with me: one, two, three. Now watch the spoon drop. Which was faster?
flow.kid: Watch the mist sparkle. Count how long it floats. Now watch the spoon drop.

ask.q: What did the mist do?
good: It sparkled and drifted slowly.
Some of it floated for a long time.

flow.parent: The spoon drop falls in a blink. The mist drifts, and some of it hangs in the beam for several seconds. Wipe the floor after.

flow.do: Ask your child what this tells us about clouds.
flow.say: A cloud is made of drops even tinier than this mist. What does that tell you about why clouds float?
flow.kid: Cloud drops are even tinier than the mist. Why do clouds float?

ask.q: Why can a cloud float?
good: Its drops are so tiny that they fall very slowly.
The air holds tiny drops up.

flow.think: If tiny drops float, how does a cloud ever make rain?

activities.title: White or Grey? Draw today's clouds
activities.context: In this activity you look at the sky from a window or balcony. You draw the clouds you see, and sort them into white and grey.

materials.item: a window or balcony with a view of the sky
paper, a pencil, and a grey and a blue crayon

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun.

setup.art: A child at a window grill looking up at a sky with white puffy clouds on one side and a dark grey cloud on the other.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the sky. Find white clouds and grey clouds.

setup.art: A sheet of paper divided into two boxes, 'white' and 'grey', with cloud drawings and tally marks in each.
setup.caption: 2. Draw them. Count them in two boxes.

flow.do: 1. Go to a window or balcony. 2. Look at the sky together, away from the Sun. 3. Point out white clouds and grey clouds.
flow.say: Look at the clouds. Which ones are white? Are any grey? Is the bottom of any cloud darker than its top?
flow.kid: Look at the sky, away from the Sun. Find white clouds. Find grey ones.

ask.q: What is different about the grey clouds?
good: They look thick and heavy.
Their bottoms are dark.
They look like rain is coming.

flow.do: 1. Fold the paper into two boxes: white and grey. 2. Your child draws each cloud they see in the right box.
flow.say: Draw each cloud in its box. Make a mark for each one. Which box has more?
flow.kid: Draw each cloud in the right box. Count them.
flow.parent: On a clear day there may be no clouds. Then draw an empty sky, and try again another day.

flow.do: Ask your child which clouds might rain.
flow.say: All clouds are made of tiny water drops. So why are some white and some grey? Which ones might rain?
flow.kid: Which clouds might rain today? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which clouds are more likely to rain?
good: The grey ones, because they are thick and full of water.

flow.parent: A thick cloud stops most of the sunlight, so its bottom looks grey. A thick cloud also holds more water, so its drops have more chances to join.

activities.title: The Window Race: watch big drops swallow small ones
activities.context: In this activity you watch drops on a window or a glass door. You see big drops race down and swallow the small drops in their way, the way drops join inside a cloud.

materials.item: a window on a rainy day, or a glass window or mirror and a spray bottle
paper and a pencil

setup.art: A rainy window with many small still drops and one big drop racing down, leaving a clear trail.
setup.caption: 1. Find a big drop at the top of the window.

setup.art: A child's finger following a big drop down the glass, counting the small drops it swallows.
setup.caption: 2. Follow it down. Count the small drops it swallows.

flow.do: 1. On a rainy day, sit by a window. 2. If it is not raining, spray a glass window or a mirror until drops form. 3. Look at the small drops and the big ones.
flow.say: Look at the drops on the glass. Which ones are moving? Which ones are still?
flow.kid: Look at the drops on the glass. Which ones move? Which stay still?

ask.q: Which drops are moving?
good: Only the big ones.
The small ones stay still.

flow.do: 1. Each of you picks one big drop near the top. 2. Follow it down with a finger held just in front of the glass. 3. Count how many small drops it swallows.
flow.say: Pick a racer. Follow it down. Count each small drop it swallows. What happens to its speed?
flow.kid: Pick a big drop. Follow it down. Count the small drops it swallows.

ask.q: What happened each time the racer swallowed a drop?
good: It got bigger.
It went faster.

flow.parent: A big drop runs down, joins the small ones in its way, grows and often speeds up. Raindrops grow the same way as they fall through a cloud.

flow.do: Write down the counts. Ask what this shows about raindrops.
flow.say: Whose racer swallowed the most? How is this like the drops inside a cloud?
flow.kid: Whose drop swallowed the most? How is this like a cloud?

ask.q: How is the window like a cloud?
good: In both, small drops join into big drops.
Big drops fall and pick up small ones on the way.

games.title: Make a Raindrop: a counting card game
games.context: This is a counting card game. Each card has some tiny drops. You join drops until you have exactly 10, and then your raindrop falls.

printables.title: 30 drop cards to cut out
items: Sun card: the Sun warms your cloud. Choose one of your drop cards. It evaporates: put it back under the pile.
Sun card: the Sun warms your cloud. Choose one of your drop cards. It evaporates: put it back under the pile.
Sun card: the Sun warms your cloud. Choose one of your drop cards. It evaporates: put it back under the pile.
Sun card: the Sun warms your cloud. Choose one of your drop cards. It evaporates: put it back under the pile.

printables.title: Raindrop score sheet
items: Raindrops made (draw one raindrop for each)

rules: Cut out the 30 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile. This pile is the cloud.
Take turns. On your turn, take the top card from the pile and put it face up in front of you. Add up all your drops.
When your drops add up to exactly 10, you have made a raindrop. It falls. Draw a raindrop on the score sheet and put those cards aside.
If your drops add up to more than 10, the drop is too big and splits. Put the card you just took back under the pile.
If you take a Sun card, choose one of your drop cards to evaporate. Put it back under the pile, with the Sun card. If you have no drop cards, just put the Sun card back under the pile.
When the pile is used up, or after 15 minutes, the player with the most raindrops wins. If you have the same number, you both win.

setup.art: A pile of small cards face down in the middle of a table, labelled 'cloud', with players sitting around it.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the cards into a cloud pile.

setup.art: A child with four cards face up in front of them showing 3, 4, 2 and 1 tiny drops, and a raindrop drawn on a score sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Join drops until you have exactly 10. Then your raindrop falls.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards with your child. 2. Shuffle them into a pile. 3. Read the rules together.
flow.say: This pile is a cloud. Each card has some tiny drops. Join drops until you have exactly ten. Then your raindrop is heavy enough to fall.
flow.kid: This pile is the cloud. Join drops until you have exactly ten. Then your raindrop falls!

flow.do: 1. Take turns taking a card. 2. Add up your drops out loud each turn. 3. Mark each raindrop on the score sheet.
flow.say: I have three and four. That makes seven. I need three more to make ten. How many do you have?
flow.kid: Take a card. Add up your drops out loud. How many more do you need for ten?

ask.q: You have 6 drops. How many more do you need to make a raindrop?
good: 4 more, because 6 and 4 make 10.

flow.parent: Help your child count on from the bigger number. Keep the cards visible so they can check.

flow.do: Count the raindrops and ask about the game.
flow.say: In the game, ten drops made a raindrop. How many tiny cloud drops make a real raindrop?
flow.kid: Ten drops made a raindrop in the game. How many in a real cloud?

ask.q: How many cloud drops make a real raindrop?
good: About a million.
Far more than ten.

flow.parent: A real raindrop holds about as much water as a million cloud drops. The game uses ten so you can count it.

games.title: Float, Join, Fall! A cloud drop moving game
games.context: This is a moving game. Everyone is a tiny cloud drop. When a card says 'Bump!', drops join hands. When a card says 'Rain!', the joined drops fall.

Take turns to turn over the top card and read it out. Everyone, including the reader, does what it says.
Drops who have joined hands move together as one bigger drop.

setup.art: Children drifting on tiptoe around a cleared room with arms out wide, and a grown-up holding up a card that says 'Float'.
setup.caption: 1. Everyone is a tiny drop. Float around the room.

setup.art: Three children holding hands crouching down and patting the floor like rain, while another child floats on tiptoe nearby.
setup.caption: 2. Bump and join. Big groups fall as rain.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space. 2. Cut out and shuffle the cards. 3. Choose who reads the first card.
flow.say: You are all tiny cloud drops. Tiny drops are light, so you float slowly. Listen for the cards.
flow.kid: You are a tiny cloud drop. Float slowly on tiptoe. Listen to the caller.

flow.do: 1. Turn over one card at a time and read it out. 2. Everyone acts it out. 3. Pass the pile to the next person after each card.
flow.say: Bump! Join hands with the drop nearest you. Now you are a bigger drop. Rain! Who is joined up and can fall?
flow.kid: Do what the card says. Join hands on Bump. Fall on Rain.

ask.q: Why can't one drop on its own fall as rain?
good: It is too small and light.
It has to join other drops first.

flow.do: Sit down together and ask about the game.
flow.say: In the game, who fell as rain? Who kept floating? Why?
flow.kid: Who fell as rain? Who kept floating? Why?

ask.q: What made a group fall?
good: It had joined enough drops.
It got big and heavy.

projects.title: Grey Sky, Rainy Day? Four weeks of sky pictures
projects.context: In this project you draw the sky once a day for four weeks, and mark whether it rained. At the end you count: do grey-cloud days bring more rain than white-cloud days?

materials.item: a notebook, or 4 sheets of paper each ruled into 7 boxes, one for each day
a grey and a blue crayon or pencil
a window or balcony with a view of the sky

projects.safety: Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Make the sky book: 28 boxes, one for each day. Draw today's sky and mark rain or no rain.
From day 2 to day 27, at the same time each day, draw the sky in the day's box. Mark a raindrop if it rained that day.
Draw today's sky. Then count: grey days with rain, grey days without, white or clear days with rain, white or clear days without.

projects.record: In each box: a quick drawing of the sky (blue for clear, white outlines for white clouds, grey for grey clouds) and a raindrop if it rained that day. At the end, a tally table with four rows.

setup.art: A notebook page with 7 small boxes, each with a quick crayon drawing of the sky, some with a little raindrop drawn in the corner.
setup.caption: 1. Each day, draw the sky in one box. Add a raindrop if it rained.

setup.art: A child counting tally marks in a table with four rows: grey and rain, grey and dry, white and rain, white and dry.
setup.caption: 2. After 4 weeks, count your tallies.

flow.do: 1. Make 28 boxes in the notebook. 2. Choose a time each day, such as after school. 3. Draw today's sky in the first box.
flow.say: Every day for four weeks, you will draw the sky. At the end we will find out: do grey skies really bring rain?
flow.kid: Draw the sky in today's box. Grey, white or blue? Did it rain?
flow.parent: Choose a month when rain is likely where you live, for example June to September in most of India, or October to December in Chennai.

flow.do: Each day, your child draws the sky and marks rain or no rain.
flow.say: Time for the sky book. What is the sky like today? Did it rain?
flow.kid: Look at the sky. Draw it in today's box. Mark a raindrop if it rained.
flow.wait: Do this once a day from day 2 to day 27. It takes about 2 minutes each day.

flow.do: 1. Make a table with four rows. 2. Count each kind of day with tally marks. 3. Ask what the numbers show.
flow.say: Let us count. How many grey days had rain? How many white days had rain? What does that tell us?
flow.kid: Count your days. Did grey days or white days bring more rain?

ask.q: Which days brought more rain?
good: Grey days, because thick clouds hold more water.
Sometimes a grey day stayed dry too.

flow.parent: You will probably find that rain came mostly on grey days. Some grey days stay dry too. A grey sky makes rain more likely, not certain.

challenges.title: A Rain Shelter for a Paper Doll
challenges.problem: Make a shelter that keeps a small paper doll dry in a 'rainstorm' of 20 sprays from a spray bottle.
constraints: The shelter must stand up on its own.
The doll must be easy to see from the side.
Test it with 20 sprays from one ruler length away.
materials: a paper doll cut from newspaper
home things to test: a plastic bag, a steel bowl, a leaf, newspaper, cardboard, foil, ice-cream sticks, tape
general: An umbrella: a cover held up on a stick.
A roof that slopes, so the rain runs off.
Plastic, which water cannot soak through.
creative: A cone of foil like a little hat, so drops run off all round.
A shelter of overlapping leaves, like the palm-leaf umbrellas once used in Kerala.
A roof with a gutter that carries the water away into a cup.
challenges.your_turn: Now build your own shelter. Test it with 20 sprays. Is the doll dry? Change one thing and test it again.

setup.art: A paper doll on a tray under a little sloping roof made of a plastic bag on ice-cream sticks.
setup.caption: 1. Build a shelter over the paper doll.

setup.art: A child spraying mist over the shelter while another child counts sprays, and drops running off the roof.
setup.caption: 2. Spray it 20 times. Is the doll dry?

flow.do: Read the problem and the rules together. Cut out a paper doll.
flow.say: Our paper doll needs a shelter from the rain. It must stand on its own and stay dry after 20 sprays. What could we use?
flow.kid: Your paper doll needs a rain shelter. It must stay dry after 20 sprays.

flow.do: Your child chooses materials and builds a shelter on the tray.
flow.say: Which things will keep water out? Which will soak it up? How will the water get away?
flow.kid: Pick your materials. Build your shelter. Where will the water go?

ask.q: Why did you choose that material?
good: Water can't soak through plastic.
A slope lets the drops run off.

flow.do: 1. Spray the shelter 20 times from one ruler length away. 2. Lift the shelter and check the doll.
flow.say: Twenty sprays. Count with me. Now let us look. Is the doll dry?
flow.kid: Spray 20 times. Count out loud. Is your doll dry?

ask.q: Where did the drops go?
good: They joined and ran off the roof.
Some soaked into the newspaper.

flow.do: Look at the usual and creative solutions together. Improve the shelter and test again.
flow.say: Here are some ideas people use. What one thing would you change? Let us test it again.
flow.kid: Look at the ideas. Change one thing. Test it again.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: a crowd of tiny drops floating in the air
a drop heavy enough to fall
water as a gas you cannot see
turn from liquid water into vapour
items.why: These are the main words of the unit. A strong answer links each word to what really happens.

items.p: Draw the steel plate after 1 spray, and again just before the first drop ran down.
items.a: First picture: many tiny dots. Second picture: fewer, bigger drops, with one starting to run.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the drops getting bigger and fewer as they join.
items.context: This question is about the spray plate test. You spray fine mist on a steel plate, one spray at a time, and count the sprays until a drop runs down.
items.art: Two empty outlines of a steel plate side by side.

items.p: A cloud is a big bag full of water that bursts when it gets too full.
items.why: False. A cloud has no bag or skin. It is millions of tiny drops floating in the air. Rain falls when the drops join into bigger, heavier drops.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the tiny drops on the plate not run down?
items.a: They were too small and light. They had to join into a bigger drop first.
items.why: A strong answer says the drops were too small, and that joining made them heavy enough.
items.context: This question is about the spray plate test. You spray fine mist on a steel plate, one spray at a time, and count the sprays until a drop runs down.

items.p: Leela, a girl in Kochi, sprayed her plate. The first drop ran down at 9 sprays. Her brother tried again, and it ran at 12 sprays. How many more sprays did her brother need?
items.why: 12 take away 9 is 3. Each try gives a slightly different number, which is why we try more than once.

items.p: Sort these into 'falls fast' and 'floats or falls slowly'.
items.why: Tiny, light things fall slowly and are easily held up by moving air. Big drops and stones fall fast.

items.p: Label the picture: sea, water vapour rising, cloud, rain.
a: Drops falling from the cloud: rain
items.why: This is where a cloud's water comes from, and where it goes. A strong answer puts the vapour between the sea and the cloud.
items.art: A simple picture of the sea with wavy lines rising, a cloud above hills, and rain falling, with four empty label lines.

items.p: Three of these are made of water. Which one is not?
items.why: Smoke from a fire is made of tiny bits of ash and gas from burning. Clouds, raindrops and mist are all water.

items.p: Anjali and Tara, two sisters in Mysuru, look at a small white cloud on a sunny day.

views.says: That cloud is full of water. It will rain soon.
It is white and thin. It won't rain from that cloud.

items.ask: Who do you agree with more? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other sister has right. Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, such as 'white clouds are thinner, so they rain less'. It also says what the other gets right, such as 'every cloud does hold water'.
items.why: Both have a point. Every cloud is made of water, as Anjali says. But a thin white cloud rarely rains, as Tara says. Thick grey clouds hold more water, and their drops have more chances to join.

items.p: On a rainy window, a big drop runs down. What happens to the small drops in its way?
opts: The big drop joins them and gets bigger
The big drop jumps over them
The small drops push the big drop back up
items.why: A big drop that meets small drops joins them and grows. Drops in a cloud grow the same way.
items.context: This question is about the window race. You watch drops on a window and follow a big drop as it runs down.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how rain is made.
items: The vapour rises and cools high up
It condenses into tiny cloud drops
The tiny drops bump and join
a: The vapour rises and cools high up
It condenses into tiny cloud drops
The tiny drops bump and join
items.why: Water goes up as invisible vapour, becomes tiny drops in the cold, and falls only after the drops join.

items.p: Ramya, a girl in your class, says, 'Clouds are made of cotton.' What would you tell her, and how could she check? Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: Clouds are made of tiny water drops. She could walk through a cloud on a hill and feel her hair get wet, or look at the mist from a spray bottle.
items.why: A strong answer gives the right idea and a real way to check it, not just 'because my teacher said so'.

items.p: Draw what you think is inside a grey rain cloud, as if you had a magic magnifying glass.
items.a: Lots of tiny drops, some joining together, and a few bigger drops falling out of the bottom.
items.why: A strong drawing shows tiny drops, drops joining, and bigger drops falling. Drawing what we can't see helps us think about it.
items.art: A big grey cloud outline with a large empty magnifying glass circle on it.

items.p: Priya and her friend Shabnam do the window race. Priya's racer drop swallowed 4 small drops. Shabnam's racer swallowed twice as many. How many did Shabnam's racer swallow?
items.why: Twice 4 is 8. The more small drops a racer swallows, the bigger it grows.
items.context: This question is about the window race. You follow a big drop down a wet window and count the small drops it swallows.

items.p: Thick grey clouds are made of dirty water, which is why they look dark.
items.why: False. Grey clouds are made of the same clear water drops as white clouds. They look dark underneath because they are so thick that little sunlight comes out of the bottom.

items.p: Match each place to when it gets most of its rain.
pairs: from June, when the monsoon arrives
very little rain in any month
items.why: Monsoon winds bring rain to different parts of India at different times. The Thar desert gets very little rain.

items.p: Label the two clouds: 'thin, lets light through' and 'thick, likely to rain'.
a: The small white cloud: thin, lets light through
The tall cloud with the dark bottom: thick, likely to rain
items.why: A thin cloud looks white because light passes through it. A thick cloud is dark underneath and holds more water.
items.art: A small thin white cloud and a tall thick cloud with a dark grey bottom, each with an empty label line.

items.p: Kavitha's family in Bengaluru wants to dry clothes on the balcony. The sky is grey in the morning.

views.says: Put the clothes out. The sky is often grey in the morning and then clears.
Keep them in. Grey clouds mean rain.
Put them out, but watch the sky and bring them in if it gets darker.

items.ask: Whose plan would you pick? Give one reason. Then say one good point in another person's plan. Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: A strong answer picks a plan and gives a reason from what we learned about grey clouds. It also names a real point in another plan.
items.why: Grey clouds make rain more likely, but not certain. Each plan weighs that risk differently. Sameer's plan uses fresh evidence: watching whether the clouds get thicker.

items.p: A cloud that is raining holds some bigger drops among its tiny drops.
items.why: Scientists flew planes through clouds and measured the drops. Clouds that were raining had bigger drops. Clouds that were not raining had almost only tiny drops.

items.p: A tiny cloud drop falls only about a centimetre each ______, so it floats.
items.why: A cloud drop is so tiny that it falls very slowly. Rising air easily holds it up.

items.p: Many people think a cloud falls when it gets heavy, like a stone. A cloud weighs as much as many elephants. Why does it stay up? Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: Its water is split into millions of tiny drops. Each tiny drop falls very slowly, and rising air holds the drops up.
items.why: A strong answer says the weight is spread over tiny drops, and that tiny drops fall slowly. The weight of the whole cloud does not pull it down like a stone.

items.p: Deepa, a girl in Madurai, sprayed her plate from far away, so less mist landed each time. What do you think happened?
opts: She needed more sprays before a drop ran down
items.why: Less water landed with each spray, so the drops took longer to grow and join. A drop still runs down in the end, once enough water has joined.
items.context: This question is about the spray plate test. You spray fine mist on a steel plate, one spray at a time, and count the sprays until a drop runs down.

items.p: Imagine a cloud where the tiny drops could never join. What would happen to the rain?
items.a: There would be no rain. The drops would stay tiny and float, or evaporate.
items.why: A strong answer uses the plate test: no joining, no big drops, so nothing heavy enough to fall.

items.p: Where does the water for a cloud come from? Sort these into 'gives water to the air' and 'does not'.
items.why: Water evaporates from seas, puddles and wet clothes. Plants give off water from their leaves too. A dry spoon or stone has no water to give.

items.p: Draw a comic strip in 3 boxes: one water drop's journey from the sea, into a cloud, and back down as rain.
items.a: Box 1: water evaporating from the sea. Box 2: a tiny drop in a cloud, joining others. Box 3: a big raindrop falling.
items.why: A strong strip shows the water rising as invisible vapour, becoming a tiny drop, joining others, and falling.
items.art: Three empty comic boxes in a row.

items.p: Three people talk about why it rains.

views.says: Rain comes when the monsoon winds bring clouds from the sea.
Rain comes when tiny cloud drops join into drops heavy enough to fall.

views.who: A girl who did the plate test
views.says: Rain comes when there are enough tiny drops in one place.

items.ask: Who is right? Can more than one of them be right? Explain. Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: A strong answer sees that all three describe part of the story: the winds bring the damp air, the drops must join, and there must be enough water.
items.why: Each person sees a different part of how rain happens. The farmer sees the wind and the season. The scientist and the girl see what happens inside the cloud.

items.p: Usha, a girl in Pune, caught raindrops in flour. She found 12 small balls, 6 medium balls and 2 big balls. How many raindrops did she catch in all?
items.why: 12 and 6 make 18, and 2 more make 20. Most were small, because only some drops grow big.
items.context: This question is about the raindrops in atta test. You hold a plate of flour in the rain for 3 seconds, and each raindrop makes a little dough ball.

items.p: Water vapour is the white, puffy stuff you see in a cloud.
items.why: Water vapour is invisible. The white you see in a cloud is made of tiny drops of liquid water.

items.p: When water vapour cools high in the sky and turns into tiny drops, we say it ______.
items.why: Condense means turn from a gas back into liquid drops. That is how every cloud forms.

items.p: Your window race showed big drops swallowing small ones. How could you test whether bigger racers run faster? Say it, and a grown-up writes it.

items.why: A strong answer compares two drops fairly, from the same place, and tries more than once.

quiz.p: What is a cloud made of?
opts: Millions of tiny drops of water
quiz.why: A cloud is made of tiny drops of water, or tiny bits of ice. Picking smoke or cotton means going by how a cloud looks from far away.

quiz.p: Why can a cloud float, even though it is made of water?
opts: Its drops are so tiny that they fall very slowly, and rising air holds them up
quiz.why: Clouds do weigh a lot. But their water is split into tiny drops that fall very slowly. The hollow bubble idea was shown wrong in 1846.

quiz.p: How does rain start inside a cloud?
opts: Tiny drops join into drops heavy enough to fall
The wind shakes the water out
quiz.why: Rain begins when tiny cloud drops grow and join. A cloud has no skin to burst.

quiz.p: Where does the water in a cloud come from?
opts: From water that evaporated from seas, rivers and wet things
quiz.why: Water evaporates into the air as invisible vapour, then cools high up into tiny drops. No new water is made.

quiz.p: Mala hangs wet clothes on her balcony in Hyderabad. By evening they are dry. Where did the water go?
opts: Into the air, as water vapour
quiz.why: The water evaporated into the air as vapour. Some day, that water may be part of a cloud.

quiz.p: Which clouds are most likely to bring rain?
opts: Thick clouds with dark grey bottoms
Small clouds on a sunny morning
quiz.why: Thick clouds hold more water, so their drops have more chances to join. They look dark because little light comes out of the bottom.

quiz.p: Why does the bottom of a rain cloud look grey?
opts: The water in it is dirty
The cloud is so thick that little sunlight gets through
quiz.why: Grey clouds are made of clear water drops, like white clouds. They are just thick enough to stop most of the light.

quiz.p: In the torch beam, which reached the floor first?
quiz.why: The big spoon drop fell in a blink. The tiny mist drops drifted slowly, the way cloud drops do.
quiz.context: This question is about the torch beam activity. You spray mist into a torch beam in a dark room, and drop one big drop from a spoon.

quiz.p: Nandini, a girl in Pune, did the spray test three times and got 10, 13 and 11 sprays. What should she say?
opts: The test failed, because the numbers are different
It always took many sprays before a drop ran down
quiz.why: Small differences are normal in any test. What all three tries agree on is the big result: tiny drops must join before they fall.
quiz.context: This question is about the spray plate test. You spray fine mist on a steel plate, one spray at a time, and count the sprays until a drop runs down.

quiz.p: About how many cloud drops does it take to make one raindrop?
quiz.why: Cloud drops are so tiny that about a million join to make one raindrop. The card game used 10 so we could count.

applications: Weather forecasters watch clouds from satellites to warn people when heavy rain is coming.
Rainwater harvesting: buildings collect rain from their roofs and send it into the ground or into tanks. Tamil Nadu made this compulsory for buildings in 2003.
Pilots fly around tall storm clouds, because the air inside them moves up and down very strongly.
Cloud seeding: scientists test spraying tiny specks into clouds to help their drops join and fall as rain.
Farmers plan when to sow their seeds by the arrival of the monsoon rains.

open_questions.q: Why do the tiny drops in some warm clouds join so quickly into rain?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can see that it happens faster than simple bumping would explain. Swirling air inside clouds probably helps, but nobody knows exactly how much.

open_questions.q: How exactly does lightning start inside a storm cloud?
open_questions.why_open: We know ice bits and drops bump and build up electric charge, but scientists still argue about how the first spark begins.

open_questions.q: How will the monsoon rains change as the Earth gets warmer?
open_questions.why_open: Warmer air can hold more water vapour, so very heavy rains may become more common. But the monsoon depends on many things, and scientists are still working out what will happen.

maths.problem: Revathi, a girl in Madurai, did the spray plate test three times. The first drop ran down at 8, 11 and 9 sprays. Which try took the most sprays? Which took the fewest?
maths.answer: The second try took the most, 11 sprays. The first try took the fewest, 8 sprays.
maths.explain: 11 is bigger than 9, and 9 is bigger than 8. The numbers are close, so every try agrees: it takes many sprays, never just one.
maths.context: This question is about the spray plate test. You spray fine mist on a steel plate, one spray at a time, and count the sprays until a drop runs down.
maths.why_maths: Putting the three numbers in order shows how close the tries were, and that the result was not just by chance.

maths.problem: In the card game, Fathima, a girl in Kozhikode, has drop cards of 3 and 4. How many more drops does she need to make a raindrop of 10?
maths.explain: 3 and 4 make 7. From 7, count on 8, 9, 10. That is 3 more.
maths.context: This question is about the Make a Raindrop card game. You join drop cards until you have exactly 10 drops.
maths.why_maths: Making 10 from smaller numbers is like tiny drops joining into one raindrop.

maths.problem: Lakshmi, a girl in Coimbatore, kept a sky book for 4 weeks. Grey sky: 10 days, and it rained on 7 of them. White or clear sky: 18 days, and it rained on 2 of them. On which kind of day was rain more likely? Draw tallies to show it.
maths.answer: Grey days. Rain came on 7 out of 10 grey days, but only 2 out of 18 white or clear days.
maths.explain: 7 out of 10 is most of the grey days. 2 out of 18 is very few of the white days. So grey skies make rain much more likely, though not certain: 3 grey days stayed dry.
maths.context: This question is about the sky book project. You draw the sky every day for four weeks and mark the days it rained.
maths.why_maths: Counting the days shows that grey skies make rain likely, not certain, which is more than a guess can tell us.

maths.problem: In the flour test, the small dough balls were 2 mm across and the big ones were 6 mm across. How many small balls would fit in a row across one big ball?
maths.explain: 2 and 2 and 2 make 6. So 3 small balls in a row are as wide as one big ball. But the big ball holds far more water than 3 small ones, because it is bigger every way: wide, tall and deep.
maths.context: This question is about the raindrops in atta test. You hold a plate of flour in the rain for 3 seconds, and each raindrop makes a little dough ball.
maths.why_maths: Comparing sizes with equal groups shows how much bigger some raindrops grow by joining.

roots.context: We have sprayed mist on a plate, watched drops race down a window and found out what a cloud is made of. Now we ask what a cloud and its rain tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: On your plate, the tiny drops from the spray clung on and did not fall. Only after many sprays did they join into a big drop that slid off. A cloud holds its water in drops too small to fall. Rain begins when many of them join into heavier drops.
deep_truth.habit: We picture a cloud as a bag or tank of rain that bursts open, and we say 'the sky opened' or 'a cloudburst'. The plate test showed that rain is made, drop by drop, by tiny drops joining.
deep_truth.evidence: In the spray plate test, one spray left tiny drops that stayed still. A drop ran down only after many sprays, once tiny drops had joined into one big drop.

three.who_am_i: Some of the water in your body once fell as rain. It was millions of cloud drops before that.
three.what_is_life: Every plant and animal, including us, lives on water that tiny drops brought down as rain. Plants also give water back to the air from their leaves.
three.what_is_this_world: The same water keeps going round: from the sea into the air, into a cloud, down as rain, into a river and back to the sea.

roots.thread: A cloud has one name, but it is millions of drops, each floating on its own. Rain begins when many of them join into one heavier drop. The raindrop lands, and later its water evaporates and spreads out into the air again. So water keeps moving between being many tiny drops and being one big drop. Everything is conscious, down to the water in a cloud, and each drop meets its neighbours as it joins them. Many scientists describe this joining with forces alone.

teachings.source: Tirukkural, chapter 2, 'The Excellence of Rain', couplet 20
teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, a Tamil poet and thinker, wrote that the world cannot go on without water, and that water comes from rain.
teachings.link: Every river and tap is filled, in the end, by rain. And rain only comes when tiny cloud drops join, as they did on your plate.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, No Death, No Fear (2002)
teachings.teaching: Thich Nhat Hanh, a Vietnamese Buddhist teacher, taught that a cloud never becomes nothing. It changes into rain, snow or ice, and goes on in a new form.
teachings.link: When a cloud rains itself away, its drops have joined and fallen. The water is still all there, in the rain, the rivers and the air.

teachings.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta (The Cloud Messenger), about the 5th century
teachings.teaching: In this Sanskrit poem, a yaksha far from home asks a monsoon cloud to carry a message of love to his wife. He talks to the cloud as someone who can travel, listen and help.
teachings.link: Kalidasa watched the monsoon clouds travel north across India. He spoke to a cloud as a someone, not a something.

science.text: One raindrop holds about as much water as a million cloud drops. Cloud drops join by bumping into each other, and in tall clouds ice helps too.
Scientists still study why drops in some warm clouds join into rain so quickly. Swirling air probably helps, but how much is not yet known.

other_view.view: They say a water drop has no awareness at all. They explain how drops join with forces between water particles, and they see no need for a mind to explain it.

practice.title: Wait for the drop
practice.say: Dip one finger in a cup of water. Hold it up, pointing down, over the cup. Keep very still. Watch the water slide to your fingertip and gather there. Breathe in and out slowly while the drop grows. When it is heavy enough, it lets go and falls. Do it three times, and breathe slowly each time.
practice.kid: Dip a finger in water. Point it down over the cup. Keep still. Watch the drop grow at your fingertip. Breathe slowly until it falls.

ask: On your fingertip, the drop waited until it was heavy enough. What do you think it is like to be a tiny drop in a cloud, waiting?
Is a cloud one thing or millions of things? Does it matter which we say?
When a cloud has rained itself away, is the cloud gone, or is it somewhere else now?

founder: ideas/by_topic/changing-materials.md, 'Clouds & Precipitation': the floating cloud dance ending in raindrop leaps (used in the Float, Join, Fall game), the drip-drip relay idea of drops joining (used in the spray plate test and the card game), cloud-spotting and recording rain (used in the white-or-grey activity and the four-week sky book).

The Class 1 weather unit says clouds are tiny drops. This unit leads on from it to how those drops become rain. The cloud in a jar, the cold tumbler and the kettle monsoon are left to the Class 3 water cycle unit.
science: Cloud droplets are typically about 10 to 20 micrometres across and raindrops about 1 to 2 millimetres, so one raindrop holds about as much water as a million cloud droplets (standard cloud physics, for example R. R. Rogers and M. K. Yau, A Short Course in Cloud Physics).
A 20 micrometre droplet falls about 1 centimetre per second in still air; a 2 millimetre raindrop falls about 6 to 7 metres per second.
Raindrop shape: small drops are nearly round, larger drops flatten at the base (high-speed photography studies, for example H. R. Pruppacher and K. V. Beard, 1970).

A. V. Waller, 'Microscopic observations on the so-called vesicular vapours of water, as existing in the vapours of steam and in clouds', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 1847 (read in 1846). He argued against the vesicle (hollow bubble) theory held by de Saussure and others.
Typical cumulus cloud water: about 500 tonnes, roughly the weight of 100 elephants (estimate by Peggy LeMone, National Center for Atmospheric Research).
Cloud seeding trials over Solapur, Maharashtra, by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune (CAIPEEX).
Tamil Nadu made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings in 2003.
Raindrops in flour: Wilson Bentley, 'Studies of raindrops and raindrop phenomena', Monthly Weather Review, 1904.

The flour test now counts its 20-minute wait, the sky-book project adds up, the spoon drop on the plate is marked as a drop that may need a second one, and each made-up child is introduced. Repeated questions and weak jokes were cut.
